subtopic: ADDRESS OF LOYALTY AND APPRECIATION OF PRESENCE ON CENTENNIAL ANNIVERSARY

speakeroldname: Right Hon. L. B. Pearson (Prime Minister):
subtopic: ADDRESS OF LOYALTY AND APPRECIATION OF PRESENCE ON CENTENNIAL ANNIVERSARY
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, as hon. members know we are to be honoured by a visit from our Queen during which, on Saturday next, she will address members of both houses of our parliament. It is most fitting that she should be present in our capital city as we commemorate the day one hundred years ago when, because of the vision and determination of some great men, our confederation passed from dream to reality.
The crown, Mr. Speaker, through Queen Elizabeth, who in her own life represents so much that is fine and good in our society, is
an integral and valued part of our constitutional structure. The monarchy symbolizes with grace and dignity the continuity of our institutions and the depth of our roots. It is a force for stability and ordered progress in our life, standing above controversy without any trace of partisanship yet adapting itself to the democratic and changing requirements and opportunities of modern life and society.
The Queen and her consort, Prince Philip, and their family have made themselves greatly admired, respected and loved by all Canadians. Their unselfish dedication and sense of duty have become a model for us all.
I am sure all hon. members would wish the Commons of Canada to extend to Her Majesty through the Speaker an expression of our loyalty and appreciation of Her Majesty's presence among us on our centennial birthday. Accordingly, Mr. Speaker, I move, seconded by the Leader of the Opposition (Mr. Diefenbaker), that an humble address be presented to Her Majesty the Queen on Saturday next, July 1, in the following words:
That an humble address be engrossed and presented to Her Majesty the Queen by the Honourable the Speaker on the occasion of the celebration of the centenary of confederation, 1st July, 1967 in the following words:

maintopic: TO HER MOST EXCELLENT MAJESTY ELIZABETH THE SECOND,

speechtext:
By the Grace of God of the United Kingdom, Canada and Her other Realms and Territories Queen, Head of the Commonwealth, Defender of the Faith:
MOST GRACIOUS SOVEREIGN:
We, Your Majesty's dutiful and loyal subjects, the	 Commons of Canada in Parliament assembled, wish humbly to convey to Your Majesty this expression of our deepest loyalty, affection and respect, and of our appreciation of the presence in Canada of Your Majesty and His Royal Highness the Prince Philip at the celebration of the Centenary of Confederation.
We pray that Your Majesty may continue to reign for many years as our gracious and beloved Sovereign.
And:
That a message be sent to the Senate informing Their Honours that the House of Commons had passed the said address and requesting Their Honours to unite with this house in the address by inserting therein the words "Senate and".

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I will tell you quite frankly that I am willing to come to an arrangement with all the members of this house. I am ready to grant the unanimous consent but on one condition. Usually, when a motion like this is brought forth, the Prime Minister is permitted to speak as well as a representative from each of the parties. Now, if I want to state that it is carried on division, then, according to standing orders, I would not be entitled to speak, since only one representative of each party is allowed to speak on motions.
When this motion is moved, if I am not allowed to speak I ask then that a 48-hour notice be given. On the other hand, if I am entitled to give my opinion on this motion and say why, if it is passed, it should be passed on division, then, so as not to frustrate all members of the house, I am ready to give unanimous consent.

speechtext: Order. I believe the hon. member does not understand the present situation. speakeroldname: Right Hon. J. G. Diefenbaker (Leader of the Opposition):
maintopic: TO HER MOST EXCELLENT MAJESTY ELIZABETH THE SECOND,
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I well recall that on October 14, 1957, when Her Majesty opened parliament she referred to the words of Elizabeth I:
Though God hath raised me high, yet this I count the glory of my crown, that I have reigned with your loves.


Then Her Majesty said:
-here in the new world I say to you that it is my wish that in the years before me I may so reign in Canada and be so remembered.
Ten years have passed. The Prime Minister stated objectively some of the things the monarchy means and some of the things it has achieved under the present Queen, the Queen of Canada. The expression "Queen of Canada" was first used by Sir John Macdonald more than 85 years ago. Some argue in favour of ending the monarchy. Sir, our freedoms, the rights of Canadians and in particular those of our compatriots who are French Canadian, were achieved by and under the British crown.

maintopic: TO HER MOST EXCELLENT MAJESTY ELIZABETH THE SECOND,
speechtext: Hear, hear.

maintopic: TO HER MOST EXCELLENT MAJESTY ELIZABETH THE SECOND,
speechtext:
That was before there was any question of Canada's independence.
[DOT] (2:50 p.m.)
It is an interesting fact of history that throughout the entire gamut of the years there has always been, in Canada, a sovereign. This was so during the days of French rule. It has been so ever since. Those who argue that the day of the monarchy is over have been answered in words which I now adopt, words of Right Hon. Vincent Massey, the first Canadian to be Governor General, when he wrote:
The monarchy Is so essential to us that without it as a bastion of Canadian nationality, of Canadian purpose and Canadian independence, we could not, in my view, remain a sovereign state.
That is the opinion of one who through the years served this nation both nationally and internationally and who occupied the position of representative of the crown.
I join with the Prime Minister in welcoming to Canada Her Majesty the Queen of Canada. The overwhelming sentiment of Canadians will be deep respect and affection; affection for a person who is well loved in her own right, and respect for the fact that she represents in terms of freedom and human dignity that something which is above political partisanship.
She is the head of our political system. As a symbol of the state she commands a loyalty which transcends any other possible symbol. Finally, as the Prime Minister stated, with her husband Prince Philip and her children she represents to all the beauty and fullness of a family in the highest degree. As Queen or as mother, in majesty or simplicity, the Queen of Canada has devoted herself to the
June 28, 1967

primary duty of the monarchy, that is service to the people. I recall the words of the first Elizabeth in 1601 when she said:
There will never queen sit in my seat with more zeal to my country, care to my subjects, and that will sooner with willingness yield and venture her life for your good and safety than myself.
Those words, spoken 400 years ago by the Queen of England, sum up the credo of service of the present Elizabeth, and I am honoured to be given the privilege of seconding this motion of loyalty to one who in her person epitomizes all that is good in the human family, one whose life has been of devotion to the service of the state.
My only hope is that from time to time in the years ahead she will again follow the course of opening the Canadian parliament and other parliaments in the Commonwealth.
I second the motion with approval and with deep sentiment.

maintopic: TO HER MOST EXCELLENT MAJESTY ELIZABETH THE SECOND,
speechtext: Hear, hear.

maintopic: TO HER MOST EXCELLENT MAJESTY ELIZABETH THE SECOND,
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, on behalf of our party I wish to join the Prime Minister and the Leader of the Opposition in welcoming Her Majesty and Prince Philip to Canada in this important year of the centenary of our confederation.
It occurred to me as a student of political science when the Prime Minister rose to pay his tribute and to move the resolution, that our democratic system in Britain, as in Canada, has in large measure been a development arising out of the original powers of the monarchy and the democratic institutions which later followed. I think the great achievement of our system has been its ability to retain the qualities of dignity, leadership and service attached to the monarchy while developing democratic rule by our people, through our parliament and the members of parliament.
For this and other reasons I am happy to associate our party with the expression of loyalty from the Prime Minister and the Leader of the Opposition to Her Majesty, to express our admiration for the dignity with which she has performed her onerous duties, and to join with other members of the house in expressing to Her Majesty and Prince Philip our deepest affection.

maintopic: TO HER MOST EXCELLENT MAJESTY ELIZABETH THE SECOND,
speechtext: Hear, hear.

maintopic: TO HER MOST EXCELLENT MAJESTY ELIZABETH THE SECOND,
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, as a French Canadian, I want to join the right hon. Prime Minister (Mr. Pearson) and the

Address to Her Majesty the Queen preceding speakers to welcome Her Majesty the Queen of England to Canada.
I do not believe that our present government, as suggested by the right hon. Leader of the Opposition (Mr. Diefenbaker) is 100 per cent monarchic. I always believed that we had a democratic government, and I believe it more and more strongly. As a matter of fact, I cannot reconcile monarchy and democracy. It is one or the other, and not both together.
As French Canadians, we must be grateful to the British crown which was, I believe, at the origin of the present constitution, the basis of confederation, the centennial of which we are celebrating in 1967.
We believe that if there were certain breaches of the constitution, as initially thought out by the British crown, it was certainly not by the British crown but by some English-speaking people who even believed at the time, 100 years ago, that the British crown was favourable to French Canadians and had, as a matter of fact, established that constitution for the benefit of the French-Canadian element in Canada.
That is why we owe a debt of gratitude to the British crown which, in my opinion, acted in a spirit of justice at that time. I hope, therefore, that Her Majesty will see for herself, when she comes to Canada, whether we have benefited from the advice she gave us the last time she was in Quebec city when she said this:
A dynamic state must not be afraid to review its political philosophy. It is not surprising that an agreement drafted a hundred years ago does not necessarily meet all the requirements of this day.
Thus, Her Majesty invited us to become adults and to leave the cradle and grow in our country. I wonder what she will think when she comes soon, and I hope that she will repeat her previous advice, so that some hon. members in the House of Commons will become adults as soon as possible and welcome as adults, independent men and great Canadians, every royal guest who will visit us.

Addressing the Canadian Club of Toronto several years ago the first native born Governor General of Canada stated four reasons for the value and importance of the crown; the crown at the head of the political system; the crown as the head of the intangible thing we call the nation; the Queen as the head of state, and the Queen with her husband and family the first family of her realm, showing us the essential unit of human society at its best.
It is with a profound feeling of pleasure and satisfaction that we in the Social Credit party support the motion just proposed by the Prime Minister and seconded by the right hon. leader of the official opposition, welcoming Her Majesty to Canada and assuring her of our affection, loyalty and respect.

maintopic: TO HER MOST EXCELLENT MAJESTY ELIZABETH THE SECOND,
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, there is a saying in British politics which goes like this: The king or the queen reigns but does not rule. This gives rise to another saying: The king or the queen can do no wrong. That is obvious, Mr. Speaker, when we speak of Her Majesty the Queen of England. This concerns, to my mind, the system and the institutions themselves rather than the person of Her Majesty the Queen of England.
We have no personal reproach to address Her Majesty, far from it. She has always been an example by her personal and public behaviour, but what I find objectionable in that motion, Mr. Speaker, is the very system represented by the British monarchy in Canada.
We can read at the beginning of this address:
By the Grace of God of the United Kingdom, Canada and Her other Realms and Territories Queen, Head of the Commonwealth, Defender of the Faith:
Mr. Speaker "Queen of the United Kingdom, Canada and her other realms and territories", this means queen of numerous independent and self-governing countries, and I feel the time has come for the North American people to assume their responsibilities as adults, as stated earlier by the hon. member for Roberval (Mr. Gauthier), and to make or, at least, bring about in our country the political changes necessary to have our independence definitely recognized.
For instance, when in 1963-64, I was a member of the Canadian delegation to the United Nations as parliamentary observer, the
[Mr. Patterson.!
present Prime Minister (Mr. Pearson) was invited or, at least, was also a member of the Canadian delegation to the United Nations, and he was not treated as a Canadian head of state, indeed not, because that role belongs exclusively to the Queen of England. I must say, Mr. Speaker, that, at that point, I felt ill at ease for the Prime Minister, the man appointed by all Canadian citizens, and who democratically represents the authority in Canada. He was not treated as head of state by the other peoples of the world. Indeed, he had to leave his seat at the back of the hall of the United Nations general assembly and cross the full length of the hall to address the other countries, while the other heads of state of the world, whether heads of small, middlesized or large countries, got what is known as the blue chair treatment; they sat in front on the platform, and only had to go from there to address the other nations of the world.
But our Prime Minister, the head of our country elected democratically by the Canadian people, the only one elected democratically by the Canadian people, could not be treated as head of state, because that is reserved solely for the Queen of England.
Well, Mr. Speaker, being a Canadian embarrassed me on that day. And, I told myself: a fundamental change must be made in our political institutions.
Our Prime Minister was not the head of state recognized by the United Nations, the Queen of England was. Mr. Speaker, if only to prove to the other nations of the world that Canada is truly independent, is not a colony, for the sake of self-respecting Canadians, a change is imperative.
Another reason, Mr. Speaker, why a change is necessary is that each time the Queen's representative attends some public event, well, England's national anthem is played before ours.
That is another situation in which Canadian citizens worthy of that name must be embarrassed, because I have been on several occasions when the national anthem of a foreign country was played instead of ours.
Why all this? Because our political institutions force us to accept that state of affairs. Well, Mr. Speaker, I protest against the use of words such as:
By the Grace of God of the United Kingdom, Canada and Her other Realms and Territories Queen, Head of the Commonwealth, etc.
I could agree to the title of "Head of the Commonwealth". "Queen of England, of the
June 28. 1967

United Kingdom, Head of the Commonwealth", I am ready to accept and recognize that. But, Mr. Speaker, I believe the constitution must be changed in Canada.
We pray that Queen Elizabeth may continue to reign for many years, I am ready to accept that. "Queen of Canada", I agree less with that, and I am not the only one in this house. There is even a Liberal member who once had the courage and boldness to confess to this, to shout it out in this house. I agree with the hon. member for Lotbiniere (Mr. Choquette), who once claimed that Canada should become a republic instead of remaining a constitutional monarchy.
Mr. Speaker, I have nothing, and I conclude with this, against the person of Her Majesty the Queen of England. On the contrary, I think that she fulfils her role magnificently as Queen of England, that she had always given a good example to all the heads of states across the world. But, I believe that it is time, in this land of America, for a people such as ours, to become adult even in spite of very strong feelings, and I quite understand that some hon. members who spoke before me may have such deep feelings. However, feelings are not enough and reason must prevail.
Mr. Speaker, it is precisely because I understand, without accepting it, however, the thinking of many others in this house, that I did not refuse unanimous consent.
This motion could have been moved on Friday and even after forty eight hours, it would have been the same. However, I want to register my disapproval with regard to that motion. If it is agreed to, I would like the words "on division" mentioned, and in the last paragraph where it says:

I should like the words "on division" to appear.
However, when the motion is presented and the words "on division" are mentioned, I pray Her Majesty the Queen of England to believe that I have nothing against her personally; on the contrary. I wish her a pleasant stay in Canada.
Many heads of state will be visiting us this year and they are all welcome. Whether it is the President of India, the President of the United States, the Queen of England, the President of the French Republic or the President of Italy, they are all welcome and I wish them a pleasant stay in our country. speakeroldname: Hon. Robert Winters (Minister of Trade and Commerce):
maintopic: STATEMENT ON GENEVA AGREEMENTS TO BE MADE ON JUNE 29
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I wish to inform hon. members that the final act of the Kennedy round agreements is being signed in Geneva on Friday morning. In view of the time difference it has been decided that the announcement of the results will be made in Canada on the preceding evening. On behalf of the Minister of Finance and myself I will be tabling in the house at 8 p.m. on Thursday, June 29, detailed information about the trade and tariff agreements concluded in the Kennedy round.
This information will also be made available to the press for release at the same time, and will be sent without delay to trade associations for distribution to individual firms across the country. I will also be mailing the material to some 150 firms which have approached us directly.

speakeroldname: Right Hon. J. G. Diefenbaker (Leader of the Opposition):

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I hope the minister will detail the detrimental effects on various industries of the adoption of a pronounced reduction in tariffs. We have a right to know before this session ends what industries will be opened to competition from abroad, what assistance is contemplated by the government for industries affected, and also what will be done in respect of workers and employees.
Competition for the domestic market will be intensified. Under this plan Canada's foreign trade will prosper only if her prices are comparable in relation to the international market-place. What will the Canadian government do to improve productivity and competitiveness? We have not had a word from this government except in speeches outside parliament. We want to know here and now before this session is adjourned what are the facts and the programs. Does the government know, or is it facing a mirage in the future,

subtopic: EFFECT OF EXPLORATION ACTIVITIES ON WILDLIFE
EFFECT OF EXPLORATION ACTIVITIES ON WILDLIFE
speechtext:
1.	Has the Canadian wildlife service or any of the government departments or agencies of the government undertaken any studies to determine the effect of mining or oil exploration activities on the natural habitat of fur-bearing animals and on the normal fish runs together with their effect on wildlife migration in the Northwest Territories and, if so, what are the results of these studies?
2.	Have the results of these studies, if any, been published and, if not, will they be, and when?

speakeroldname: Hon. Judy V. LaMarsh (Secretary of Slate):
subtopic: EFFECT OF EXPLORATION ACTIVITIES ON WILDLIFE
speechtext:
In so far as the Department of Fisheries is concerned:
1.	Department of Fisheries personnel have made observations during oil, seismic, exploration surveys. Exploration companies take precautions to avoid fish kills as stipulated by the department. No serious fish kills have been observed in the Northwest Territories.
2.	No. No.
In so far as the Department of Indian Affairs and Northern Development is concerned:
1.	This issue has arisen many times before and in the past has resulted in minor investigations reported by a memorandum from or to initiating agencies. We have been made aware of the following occurrences which may be construed as damage to wildlife habitat: (a) The destruction of lichen tundra by tracked vehicles-Recovery may take many years and tracked vehicles except those with very low ground pressure appear to be the biggest offenders. Most exploration companies are aware of this problem and there have been few complaints, (b) Councillor Robert Porritt of the Northwest Territories council has registered concern over the effect of staking in the Pine Point area on trapping and wildlife habitat. The amount of line cutting between Hay River and the Wood Buffalo national park boundary is quite extensive, but the detrimental effects on wildlife have not been assessed. The area is almost uniformly wet and boggy and openings effected

by line cutting would dry some of the area and probably increase the amount of browse for ungulates. On the other hand, slash left by line cutting crews on ponds and streams reduces their suitability as muskrat and beaver habitat. This type of damage was investigated in Wood Buffalo national park by the Canadian Wildlife Service and commercial logging opertors were instructed to desist, (c) The Canadian Wildlife Service has alerted water carriers on the Athabasca river to report any pollution of the Athabasca and Slave rivers by effluent from the oil extraction plant at Bitumont, Alberta. Any oil travelling downstream could seriously affect waterfowl populations in Wood Buffalo national park and elsewhere and could also be detrimental to fish populations. At present, there is no evidence of pollution from this source, (d) The numbers of forest fires attributed to mining exploration crews have not been determined. It was felt that although the numbers may have been significant in the past, such crews are now obligated to carry fire fighting equipment of their own to reduce the incidence.
2.	Present studies have not been intensive enough to warrant publication at present. It is expected that in the near future, a more systematic survey of this problem will be done and the material published.

speechtext:

It provides for the development and maintenance of mooring basins and harbours for pleasure craft, principally through the construction of breakwaters, and through dredging.
Projects will be undertaken only where there is a commitment by private, municipal or other local interests to develop shore facilities within the harbours so created.

Mr. Chairman, the other day I listened to the minister's statement in introducing his estimates. Like so many of his statements it was full of assurance, reassurance and statistics. From it we could assume that the nation was in an excellent state so far as health and welfare are concerned. But one recalls previous statements made by the Minister of National Health and Welfare, also-full of hope but not matched by performance after they were made. I am afraid that when we examine these estimates we see several areas where concern must be expressed about the performance in implementing previous announcements by the minister.
I mention in particular the old age security supplement, of which the minister spoke with considerable pride, as well he might, because it was his idea to establish a guaranteed annual income supplement and at the time it was a major change of policy. But as one examines how the income supplement is being administered across the country it becomes more and more clear it was the government's intention to have the Canada Assistance Plan take care of the increase in old age security pension payments. However, when it became obvious that this intention was impossible to carry out, and indeed was
June 28, 1967

Supply-Health and Welfare extremely unwise, politically, the guaranteed annual income supplement was introduced.
In the minister's statement we were given the statistics respecting some 700,000 old age security pensioners who were receiving payments and some 430,000 who were receiving payment in full. It would be interesting to know how many in all applied for the guaranteed annual income supplement, how many were refused, and how many of those who had been receiving some supplement in the form of a veterans allowance payment were rejected. This kind of detail would be very meaningful in examining the success of the guaranteed annual income plan. I am afraid that for many pensionable Canadians it was not much of a guarantee. There was a real contradiction between what they were told in the green instruction booklet sent to them and what happened when they applied for the supplement. Further, there was a real difference between what we were told in this chamber during debate on the supplement and what subsequently happened in relation to the veterans allowance supplement and to provincial supplements being paid by some of the provinces.
We had a pretty solemn assurance from the minister last December on how the supplement plan was to be implemented. He used words like these, Mr. Chairman, and I quote from Hansard of December 8, 1966, page 10896:
They will not suffer any indignity, if this can be called an indignity, and I do not think it is. They will not be asked to do anything that a corporation president is not asked to do, or any other person in the country, in the way of providing information with respect to income or having the accuracy of that return checked.
Further, as recorded on page 10898 he said:
We are doing this without the application of the much dreaded and odious means test. There is no possible comparison between the simple declaration which must be filled out merely asking applicants to list items of income under the Income Tax Act, and a means test. If the program embodied a means test in the way in which it has been administered in the provinces I would not be recommending it to the House of Commons. This is not a means test. It merely asks the old age pensioners to fill out a simple form listing the items of income which they would normally list if they were filling an income tax return. I see no indignity or loss of self-respect in the process.
At the time, Mr. Chairman, I did not see any indignity or loss of self-respect in the process but now I do see a great deal of indignity resulting from the actions of the Department of National Health and Welfare in conjunction with the Department of Veterans Affairs. People who have applied for


the guaranteed income supplement have discovered that the veterans affairs means test is applied rigidly and that the veterans allowance they are being paid is taken out of the guaranteed annual supplement. Putting it the other way around, the supplement is not a guaranteed annual one and their veterans allowance is cut. Either way you look at it, this is what happens, e (4:10 p.m.)
The old age security pensioners were told not to list that item. If they go ahead and list it they end up with monthly payments which are less than they were before. When this is taken into account they suddenly find they do not receive the monthly amount they were receiving before. I realize that the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre has come around to seeing some good lately in a guaranteed annual income and I trust that he and the minister are looking into this concept jointly for the future. Let me suggest seriously to the minister that if he really would like to obtain the greatest amount of political advantage from hospital grants he should reexamine the structure of the grants and revise them in accordance with the increase in the cost of hospital construction. This increase in the cost can be laid at the feet of this same government which chose to impose an exhorbitant and inflationary tax on construction materials, thereby showing absolutely no restraint in taxing construction. This has caused a greater spiralling of construction costs, including the construction of hospitals, than anything else.
An examination of these grants should have been made long ago. With the implementation of full medicare and the resulting demands that will be made on the hospitals of this country, it is scandalous that no changes have been made in the schedule of these grants. When the people read the statements of the minister regarding his promises for medicare they will be lulled into the false assurance that their medical needs will be taken care of after 1968. However, when they go or attempt to be admitted to hospital after 1968 they will learn that space is simply not available. Whether or not doctors will be available is doubtful, but the space will not be available and medicare will be meaningless for them because the groundwork has not been laid. They will be victims of the same illusion that some of the old age security pensioners laboured under when they accepted the promises that some of their problems would be alleviated by this government but later learned to their sorrow that promises and the implementation of them are not always the same.
Finally I should like to refer to what is perhaps a minor part of the spending of the department, that on grants for fitness and amateur sport. We in this country are proud of our contribution to amateur sport and our efforts in a great many fields, some of which we consider particularly Canadian. We have been particularly proud of our efforts in the field of hockey and extremely proud of our recent ski teams. However, compared to what happens in many nations of the world, our approach to these things on the governmental level cannot even be considered amateurish, but only rather infantile.
In this respect, although we had a sharp increase from 1964 to 1967 in the estimates

there has been no increase this year. We know there are any number of governments in the world which set out deliberately as national policy to have the finest teams of athletes to take part in various competitions in the world that they can possibly send. This is done as government policy. We in Canada apparently feel that the system we used 30 or 40 years ago can still work. We send our teams and, with rare exception, we are disappointed with the results. Our hopes are raised in respect of world championships, but we invariably lament the fact that we no longer can maintain our standard.

We are not asking here for an out and out subsidy but for a grant which would be large enough to allow the fitness council to do some of the things they would like to do and should be able to do.
For example, let us consider a sport that is of importance to my constituents, namely skiing. They would like to know in advance what grants could be allocated to meet the many demands over a period of three years, because it is very difficult to get the team together and to keep it together when the committee organizing the meet applies for the grant and does not know until very late in the game whether or not it will receive it. Mr. Chairman, I want to take advantage of the debate on the estimates of the Department of National Health and Welfare to say a few words about some of the committee reports which are so seldom debated in the House of Commons. First of all, I want to say a few words about the health and welfare committee and its hearings last year on birth control. As I am sure all hon. members of the house are aware, the committee recommended that the words "preventing conception or" be removed from the Criminal Code, the effect of which would be to make the dissemination of knowledge and the sale of contraceptives legal in Canada. I must say that during its hearings the committee was greatly concerned about the fact that if these words were taken out of the Criminal Code there might be some trouble with the advertising of contraceptives which would be considered to be in bad taste and the indiscriminate sale of contraceptives in various stores which again would be in very bad taste. The committee made some very sensible recommendations regarding a few amendments of a simple nature to the Food and
June 28, 1967

Supply-Health and Welfare Drugs Act which would cover the sale and advertisement of contraceptives.
I should like to say as a member of that committee which adopted the report almost unanimously, a report which in my view reflects the feelings not only of members of this House of Commons but of the people of Canada, that I would be quite shocked and surprised if the government did not carry out the recommendations which that committee made. I certainly expect it will do so in the fall when amendments to the Criminal Code, about which we have been told, will be brought about.
In that connection I should like to say a few words about a subject which has not been discussed in the committee to date, namely, the matter of abortion. When the committee met on the question of birth control it was understood by the committee that they would be dealing solely and specifically with the question of birth control and not the question of abortion. The two matters are completely separate and should not be considered together or confused.
As the house is aware, yesterday several private members' bills dealing with abortion were sent to the committee on health and welfare which now has that reference before it. It is hoped the committee will meet soon in view of the fact that representations have already been made to various members of the committee, and hearings should be held in the fall. It is hoped that during the summer recess the people who are interested in the subject of abortion will have two or three months in which to prepare briefs and get ready for an appearance before the committee which should sit early in the fall. I believe that full and detailed hearings will be necessary. I think most people in Canada agree that some changes with regard to abortion are necessary in the Criminal Code, but there are a great many different opinions as to how far these changes should go and how they should be brought about.
I should like to devote most of my remarks to the special committee on drug costs and prices which reported to this house on April 3 of this year. However, before I get into that subject to any great extent I should like to say a few words about the 12 per cent federal sales tax on drugs which, as the Minister of Finance mentioned in his budget, would be taken off the price of drugs as of September 1 of this year. Hon. members will note that the report of the committee did not recommend that the sales tax should come off all drugs

but that it should come off prescription drugs only. It is my understanding that the government removed the sales tax from all drugs because it was administratively very difficult to take if off one form of drugs only and it would also create great difficulties for a doctor to whom a patient might say "I know I can buy such and such a drug over the counter without a prescription, but if you give me a prescription for it I can buy it without having to pay the federal sales tax." This would mean a great deal of paper work for the doctor. I thought the government made a wise decision in removing the tax from all drugs.
[DOT] (4:40 p.m.)
The reason, of course, that the effective date is September 1 is to allow the drugs now on the druggists' shelves, and on which tax has been paid, to be used up. A druggist always has to keep a large stock of drugs on hand to meet any demand, and these stocks will not be used up by the time the change is made on September 1. Unless a druggist is willing to absorb the loss on these stocks, prices will not automatically fall on September 1, 1967. As is mentioned many times in the report of the committee on drug prices, the prices of drugs will not fall 12 per cent when the 12 per cent federal sales tax is removed.
I should like to put on the record two paragraphs from the report of the joint committee on drug costs and prices, starting at page 30:
From these figures one might be inclined to conclude that elimination of sales tax could result in an average reduction of 5 to 10 per cent in the price of drugs to the consumer, depending upon the particular pricing method in use. However, reduction in prices is not ensured simply by the elimination of the sales tax. This point was emphasized by many who made representations to the committee. It was pointed out that the elimination of the federal sales tax should be taken as part of a program to reduce drug prices and that this can be better assured by introducing competition into the drug market. Evidence, for example, has been shown that tariff reductions have not always been accompanied by a corresponding decrease in the price of drugs although the cost to the manufacturer was lower.
Both the drug manufacturers and retail pharmacists offered the opinion before the committee that the benefits of a reduction in sales tax would be passed along to the consumer. However, the committee concludes that, without more effective operation of competitive forces than presently exists in the drug industry in Canada, the only certain result from removal of the tax would be a reduction in costs to the manufacturers. The consumer must also understand that the removal of the 12 per cent federal sales tax on drugs will not, (however much drug manufacturers and retail
June 28, 1967

pharmacists honestly co-operate), lower the price of drugs 12 per cent for the reasons already discussed in this section.
_ Since the publication of this report, Mr. Chairman, we have heard rumours that drug prices either have gone up or will go up prior to September 1 so that there will be no effect from the removal of the sales tax. I personally, along with many other members of the committee, have had a great deal of interest in this subject. I have taken pains to make as many detailed inquiries as I could concerning this rumour. I must say I have found no evidence at all other than the case of one drug by the name of demerol, which is a narcotic that is not prescribed very widely nor it is very expensive. I feel it is only fair to the drug manufacturers and pharmacists to point out these facts. I have found no evidence that drug prices have gone up or will go up. As a matter of fact, I am told no increase in drug prices will take place now after all the adverse publicity. I should point out that one of the companies brought about a reduction in the price of a fairly expensive antibiotic during the hearings of the drug committee.
As I know all members are aware, the special committee made 23 recommendations, which we refer to as a package deal, to bring down the cost of drugs. Generally speaking, the recommendations contained in the report can be divided into two sections, each of which emphasizes a basic idea. The first section of these recommendations to lower drug prices would make cheaper drugs available in Canada or make drugs manufactured in Canada less expensive. Fifteen of these recommendations were designed for that purpose.
The second group contains six recommendations, and these are designed to make sure that if available drugs are cheaper or if cheaper drugs are available-I am sure hon. members will see the distinction-they meet the requirements for safety established by the food and drug directorate. There were three other recommendations made in the report which probably have no effect on the first two groups but which the committee felt might be useful.
I should point out that while lower drug prices are important, they are of no use if the drugs are not prescribed. I should point out too that the report itself is not worth the paper it is written on if we cannot convince the medical profession that they can safely prescribe the drugs that are available in Canada. Less expensive drugs must not be 27053-133J

Supply-Health and Welfare less safe. We must do what we can to bring down prices but we cannot do that by sacrificing the safety or the quality of our drugs. There is no question but that less expensive drugs are available in Canada now. If one has any doubt about this, one has only to look at the practice of the government of Canada and most of the provinces in tendering. I am pleased to say that there was no evidence before the committee that any significant problem dealing with the safety of drugs had been introduced since the government began issuing the requirements for drug firms tendering on a particular drug.
These requirements come under the Canadian government specification board and are called standards for manufacture, control and distribution of drugs. Certainly the drugs purchased by the government are cheaper because no federal sales tax is paid on them, but the saving as a result of tendering on drugs goes far beyond that. The inspection of drugs intended for government use or public use comes under the food and drug directorate.
It seems to me that cheaper drugs can be made available because the inspection services are the same. I feel that to ask doctors to change their prescribing habits would be a very serious responsibility, but the committee undertook it and eventually the government will have to take that responsibility. When the doctor prescribes drugs he wants to be sure they are safe. I should point out, and I am sure every member of the committee is aware, that any drug can kill if it is taken in large enough doses. Some drugs can kill even if they are taken in the prescribed manner because the person may develop an idiosyncrasy or allergic reaction. As a result of my experience I can say that no drug is ever prescribed or taken lightly by the medical profession.
In order to ensure knowledge of drugs and their safety, the committee also recommended that a bulletin be published and that copies of it be given free to the doctors. It should be published by the federal government and sent to the doctors monthly. Here I would include the following information which is found in the report on page 17, and this information should be contained in the publication:
(i)	Generic name of the drug
(ii)	Names of all manufacturers of the drug, and brand names of the above drug
(iii)	Comparative costs and clinical equivalency of the above drugs
(iv)	Therapeutic action of drug
(v)	Side effects of drug, contra-indications and toxicity
June 28, 1967

Supply-Health and Welfare
(vi)	Last assay for each company's product, of content and availability of active ingredient, solubility and disintegration
(vii)	Any problems with any company's product toxicity, impurity, seizures, court actions, failure to meet standards, etc.
4f this bulletin were published it would provide the doctor with knowledge of all the products which were available on the Canadian market, how safe they were and how much they would cost in each case. I am convinced that cheaper drugs, or perhaps a better expression is less expensive drugs, can be made available in Canada, first of all, by importing cheaper drugs. The committee made many recommendations concerning trade mark and patent changes. If these were carried out as recommended by the committee the importing of cheaper drugs would be possible.
[DOT] (4:50 p.m.)
I know that the drug manufacturing industry in Canada is afraid that if these recommendations were carried out the industry would suffer a great deal and perhaps disappear. I do not agree with that view at all. I think it is a very live industry and that it would drop its prices and be forced to compete. Bringing in cheaper drugs from outside Canada, provided they were safe-and the committee report took that into account -would inject competition into a relatively non-competitive market as it exists at the present time.
The second way that less expensive drugs could be made available in Canada is by lowering the cost of the drugs that are actually manufactured in Canada. One of the startling things to committee members, I think, was when it was revealed that approximately one third of the manufacturers' dollar in Canada actually goes on marketing and promotional expenses.
Reference was made in this debate earlier and also in the committee hearings to a recommendation in the Hall report concerning marketing expenses, and I should like to put it on the record. I read from page 22 of the committee report on drug costs and prices:
The Hall commission likewise came to the conclusion that marketing expenses in the drug industry were too high, and recommended a compulsory method whereby this expense might be lowered, namely, "that in the application of the provisions of the corporation Income Tax Act to the manufacturers, importers and distributors of drugs, consideration should be given to establishing a maximum of 15 per cent of total sales as the allowable deductible expense for advertising, sales promotion, 'detail men', and other similar items",

The committee did not agree with the Hall commission on this point, and in explanation of that disagreement I want to put on the record a sentence in our report. If I may again quote the committee report, in the next paragraph there appears this passage:
Yet again, regardless of the savings hopefully expected as a result of the recommendation, it might well be that the drug companies would, regardless of increased taxes, press their promotional activity to meet the continued competition of their rivals-which might easily result in higher costs at the manufacturers' level, and then higher drug costs to the consumer.
So the committee felt that the recommendation of the Hall commission would actually tend to increase the price of drugs rather than lower it.
We often hear a great deal about the question of quality control or safety of drugs. Evidence put before the committee showed that this is not a feature of great cost; therefore the question of safety is not a debatable one. There is nothing in this report that would jeopardize the safety or quality of any drug. To use safety as an argument for the high cost of drugs is just not acceptable.
In summary, Mr. Chairman, what the report really says is that price competition is the answer in the Canadian drug market, not product competition between companies as now exists, with the accompanying high marketing and promotional costs. As I mentioned earlier, this is a package deal. The recommendations made in the report would mean changes to the Food and Drugs Act, the Customs Act, the Patent Act, the Trade Marks Act and, as I have already said, there have been changes made in the budget.
The federal government actually has no power to carry out many of the recommendations which have been made, but we certainly hope that those who have jurisdiction in these areas will carry out their own investigation based on our recommendations. Personally I am convinced-and I think the members of the committee are too; the report was adopted unanimously-that less expensive but safe drugs are possible in Canada. I ask the government, and in particular the Minister of National Health and Welfare and the Registrar General who are responsible for implementing many of these recommendations, to bring in the necessary legislation early this fall.

speechtext:
That, in the opinion of this house, the government should consider the advisability of establishing an inland waterway from Winnipeg through Selkirk to Edmonton, via the Red River, Lake Winnipeg and the Saskatchewan River.

DEBATES	June 28, 1967
He said: Mr. Speaker, I had this same motion on the order paper last year and it came up for discussion on June 1, 1966. As the government has not taken any action on it, I felt duty bound to place it on the order paper again.
I am happy that there is an opportunity again to discuss the merits of this motion. All I am requesting is that the government should give consideration to the advisability of establishing an inland waterway from Winnipeg through Selkirk to Edmonton via the Red River, Lake Winnipeg and the Saskatchewan River. This is not an unreasonable request. I hope that the Minister of Transport particularly, as a former Manitoban, will lend his support to this motion and not let another year go by without initiating a feasibility study of this proposed waterway.
When speaking on this resolution last year the hon. member for Red Deer (Mr. Thompson) said he would have been happier if I had specified that one end of the system be Rocky Mountain House. I would have no objection to this. In fact the Voyageurs, one of Canada's centennial projects, started from Rocky Mountain House in the foothills of the Rockies on the North Saskatchewan River and will finish at Expo in Montreal. The Voyageurs will arrive in Selkirk, Manitoba, on Sunday, July 2. Besides being greeted by the residents of Selkirk, many other people will be there to greet them, including Lord and Lady Selkirk. Those participating in the centennial canoe pageant will be familiar with the terrain along this proposed waterway and they will be a valuable source of information for compiling the merits and feasibility of this system.
I pointed out last year that the first promoter of this proposed waterway to whom I listened was the late Mr. J. F.-Fergie- Cunningham, who had personally carried out research and study of this system. He firmly believed that it would be practical. Subsequently the Selkirk Chamber of Commerce took up the promotion of this proposed inland waterway and did an excellent promotional job. So far, however, there has been no government action. If one firmly believes in a project and does not immediately meet with success, one should not give up but should continue to promote the project and request the government to take action.

perseveres long enough, one generally meets with success in the end.
The purpose of this proposed waterway is to provide another means of transportation. It is only natural that some of those engaged in other modes of transportation will oppose this proposition and even ridicule it. I personally believe that this proposed western inland waterway will reduce freight costs in the prairie provinces, will accelerate development in northern areas and will encourage production of minerals as well as agricultural and forest products. It will open new frontiers to recreation and will encourage tourists to come to these areas. It will help to bring in much needed United States dollars and thus help to rectify the imbalance of trade with our neighbour to the south. In addition, it will shorten the distance for building roads to resources and will create substantial additional employment.
Many have said to me that this idea of a western inland waterway is a very good one but that before it will be practical or feasible we need a much larger population and much more industrial development. I do not dispute the fact that this is probably correct. The population of Canada from now on will increase at a much faster pace than in the past and the same applies to industry. With an increasing population, industrial development will take place at a far greater place than in the past. In view of this I feel it is imperative that the government start now with studies and not wait until we require this additional transportation system.
It is a foregone conclusion that extensive population growth and extensive industrial growth will take place in the three prairie provinces in the years ahead. The prairies have wheat, oil, potash, minerals, agricultural products, pulp and forest products, fish, and so on. For these reasons this is a natural area for industry to establish and a western inland waterway will help to bring industry there.
[DOT] (5:10 p.m.)
In the period from 1870 to 1917 many boats travelled the Saskatchewan River system. There was no expenditure made for river improvement. Some of these boats were of a good size, as long as 200 feet. We have today a fleet of tugs and barges operating on Lake Winnipeg. I am told that this is the most up-to-date equipment of its kind on the North American continent. During the construction of the hydro development at Grand Rapids this fleet moved a lot of material and equipment to that power site. These crafts
Establishment of Inland Waterway will be ideal for operating on an inland waterway such as I visualize.
An extensive detailed investigation to ascertain the feasibility and cost of providing a navigable waterway for vessels and barges to operate between Edmonton and Lake Winnipeg was carried out between June, 1910 and October, 1915. The complete report of this investigation was submitted in November, 1917 by the chief engineer of the Dominion Public Works Department. This report, based upon a minimum of six feet of water at mean low water levels from Lake Winnipeg to Edmonton, estimated the cost as follows: Dredging and channel improvement, $6,200,000; seven locks and dams, $14,565,591; total, $20,765,591. When this report was received the first world war was in progress. Then came the post-war years, the depression and the second world war. No action was taken on the report.
Mr. Speaker, bearing in mind that it is over 40 years since the last study of the proposed inland waterway was made I would urge the Minister of Transport or the Minister of Public Works, or both of them, to initiate a study at this time in order that up-to-date figures may be available. At the time of the previous study the economy of western Canada was centred on wheat and other grains. Now, western Canada is becoming industrialized and, as I have pointed out, industrial development will from now on expand at a much more rapid pace. It is essential to have competitive transportation systems which will be able to provide low-cost transportation service. I believe that in the future a multi-transportation service which will include highway, rail, air and waterways will be needed to serve the needs of the people.
Following the second world war, tremendous developments of waterways have taken place in the United States, in Europe and in other parts of the world. The St. Lawrence seaway was built after the second world war and now permits ocean liners to sail to the lakehead.
In the June issue of Ship-Shore News there is an article under the following headings, "Canal Traffic And City Will Benefit From $350 Million Dig". It reads in part as follows:

Thank you, Mr. Speaker, I thought I was allowed 20 minutes.

The Moselle Waterway, a 170-mile link between the steel producers of Lorraine and the Rhine, was officially opened in 1963. The construction of this waterway was an engineering feat of some note and the cost was shared by three countries, France, West Germany and Luxembourg. This inland waterway enabled the French steelmakers to ship steel to prospective customers in southern Germany more cheaply than before. It also enabled them to bring in coal by barge from the Ruhr area and from Holland and this means lower freight rates. This inland waterway is helping the economies of the three participating countries.
The proposed inland waterway from Winnipeg through Selkirk to Edmonton is approximately 1,200 miles long. The type of waterway I have in mind, suitable for tugs and barges to use, would not require any great depth of water and would therefore not require any great amount of digging. Every power development creates a lake; I am thinking of the power developments at Grand Rapids and at Squaw Rapids. The formation of these lakes should make navigation easier. There will be locks needed at the dam. From an engineering point of view there should be no problem about making this inland waterway a reality.
During the past year, construction of a pulp and paper mill at Prince Albert has been started and another pulp and paper mill and a forest products plant are under construction at The Pas, Manitoba. Some time in the future, another pulp and paper mill may be established at Grand Rapids.
At the present time Marine Transport hauls pulpwood by tug and barge to the pulp and paper mill at Pine Falls. Some of the pulp-wood is hauled in from north of Norway House on the Nelson River. The Selkirk Silica Sand Company hauls silica sand from Black Island in Lake Winnipeg to Selkirk where the sand is processed. It is logical to suppose that eventually there will be a glass factory established alongside the sand processing plant. Under the ARDA-FRED agreement, there will be an industrial park established in Selkirk. In considering the future development of Selkirk, one must not discount the possibility that some day Selkirk may be situated on a great inland waterway. At the present time most of the lake traffic on Lake Winnipeg funnels out from Selkirk. In the future water traffic may greatly increase and become far more important than it has been in the past. No doubt an inland waterway could be established from Lake Winnipeg to
June 28, 1967

the Great Lakes. This is the route which the explorers travelled.
[DOT] (5:20 p.m.)
I can also visualize a waterway from Lake Winnipeg to Hudson Bay. With power development now taking place on the Nelson River, consideration should be given to the possibility of making the Nelson River into a navigable waterway. If these waterways become a reality then Selkirk will become a busy inland seaport.
Recently I had the privilege of attending the official opening of the new melt facilities at the Manitoba rolling mills in Selkirk. These new, modern facilities cost the company over $9 million. The modernization of this plant is an indication that this company has faith in Manitoba and in the town of Selkirk. Also recently I attended sod-turning ceremonies for the distillery which the House of Seagram is building at Gimli, Manitoba. The establishing of this distillery at Gimli involves an expenditure of $10 million. This is an indication that the House of Seagram has faith in Manitoba and in the town of Gimli.
Lake Winnipeg is by far the largest producer of fresh water fish in western Canada. The fish are brought in by boat to the fishery plants at Gimli, Selkirk and Winnipeg. Canadian forces base Gimli is a very active base where jet pilot training is carried out. Indications are that this base will be active for many years to come. The Pan-American sailing races are being held at Gimli this summer. I merely point these things out, Mr. Speaker, to show that business has confidence in this area of Manitoba and that exciting things are already taking place.
I urge the government to take steps to ascertain the transportation needs of western Canada for the next 10, 20 or 30 years. I am personally convinced that the time will come when inland waterways will become an important part of our transportation needs. Perhaps the government will prefer to conduct a study of the whole water system in western Canada, including source and supply, conservation, power development and inland waterways. If the government is prepared to do this I will be satisfied provided such a survey or study is initiated at an early date.

Mr. Speaker, first I would like to assure my good friend that I do not intend to ridicule his idea. On the contrary, the hon. member is to be commended for his perseverance in bringing up again the subject of the motion under
Establishment of Inland Waterway discussion which was debated in the house, as he stated, on June 1, 1966.
This motion, which requests the government to give consideration to the advisability of establishing an inland waterway from Winnipeg through Selkirk to Edmonton via the Red River, Lake Winnipeg and the Saskatchewan River was first placed on the order paper in March, 1962. Even older than the hon. member's motion of 1962 is an engineering survey of this project which was first made by the Department of Public Works more than half a century ago, in the years 1910 to 1914. Then, of course, the first great war broke out and the scheme was abandoned for the duration of the war. Afterwards other things happened to curb the enthusiasm of those who favoured the idea at that time. It is quite conceivable that if the first world war had not intervened the scheme envisaged by those involved in that study might have had a chance of receiving serious consideration by the government of the day.
The report of the 1910-1914 engineering survey, based upon a minimum of six feet of water at mean low water levels from Lake Winnipeg to Edmonton, estimated that the cost would be in the order of $6,200,000 for dredging and channel improvement, and for other improvements $14,565,591, making a total of $20,765,591.
I believe I mentioned in my previous speech on this motion the plan of Mr. John R. MacNichol, former M.P. His plan was to make the old fur trade route navigable for coal and oil transport, something which the hon. member for Selkirk seems to be advocating also or, in other words, that this particular plan be revived. Another interesting scheme suggested by a Professor Hind of the University of Toronto in the 1870's was to pipe water across the prairies to the cities of Moose Jaw and Regina, which would have meant the construction of a dam and a diversion of the Elbow River, with the possibility in mind of travelling by boat all the way from Winnipeg to Calgary.
However, none of these schemes materialized, and in 1961 the premier of Manitoba requested a review of the information obtained in the survey which was made before 1914. At this time the review concerned the engineering and economic problems associated with the canalization of the Saskatchewan River to determine the justification for a detailed engineering survey, including field investigation, preliminary design and, of course, cost estimates.
June 28. 1967

Establishment of Inland Waterway
The 1961 survey concluded that there would not be a sufficient volume of traffic to provide significant transportation savings to set against the heavy capital and operational costs which would be involved for the federal government in the construction of such a waterway. I venture to say that the 1961 survey holds true today. The road and rail transportation systems now in existence would appear to be capable of meeting foreseeable future requirements.
When this transportation system was first suggested the prairie provinces did not have the facilities which exist today. At that time the railway and the waterways were the main transportation systems. The trans-Canada highway now provides a direct first class route for interprovincial truck and passenger traffic, and our air lines offer excellent passenger, freight and air express service between all major points.
Although the 1910-1914 engineering survey was confined to the route from Edmonton to Winnipeg and did not investigate the potential of the South Saskatchewan for navigation, it is still considered adequate for determining the order of magnitude of the costs involved in developing either or both the north and south branches of the Saskatchewan River for navigation purposes.
The engineering survey of 1914, as I stated before, estimated the cost of providing navigation facilities from Edmonton to Lake Winnipeg at approximately $20 million. In 1961 the revised costs, based on the original plan, had sky-rocketed to an estimated $100 million. I shall leave it to my hon. friend to imagine the cost six years later.
[DOT] (5:30 p.m.)
It is extremely doubtful that present circumstances would result in a substantial downward revision of these costs. It was stated that the 1961 estimated cost of $100 million could possibly be $250 million if the project was completed today. It might be noted that one estimate is in respect of a navigation route using the North Saskatchewan River and that the other is in respect of a navigation route using the South Saskatchewan River. However, the review carried out in 1961 for the previous minister of northern affairs and national resources found that it was reasonable to assume that a minimum cost to develop a navigation route originating either on the North or South Saskatchewan river and ending at Lake Winnipeg would be in the neighbourhood of
[Mr. Badanal.l
$100 million and could possibly be $250 million. It naturally follows that if the expenditure of the estimated $100 million cannot be justified on the basis of potential transportation savings, any further studies conducted at the present time are not warranted.
In 1961 the estimated cost was $100 million to $250 million, and if the lower figure is amortized on a 50-year basis, having in mind the economic factors which are involved, the equivalent annual costs, including interest and amortization, would be some $5,500,000. On the higher figure of $250 million the annual costs would be $13,750,000. Neither of these amounts includes maintenance or operating expenses.
The estimated physical capacity of the locks in the proposed system would possibly be nine million tons of freight annually. This assumption is made on the basis of equal traffic in both directions, which is highly improbable. It appears that by far the greatest volume of traffic that would move on such a waterway would be bulk cargoes such as coal, petroleum products and grain. These would be the main cargoes on the waterway during the estimated seven-month season and, as I said before, these main cargoes would probably move from west to east with little apparent backhaul traffic in sight.
With the estimated physical capacity of the locks set at nine million tons of freight annually, and the greater portion of the freight moving eastward, it would be possible to handle only 4.5 million tons one way. This figure is based on continual operation of the locks during the seven-month season. Therefore a more realistic figure on the capacity of the system would be approximately three million tons a year.
The future estimated requirements of the Manitoba Hydro-Electric Power Board for coal during the next 10 to 20 years are approximately one million tons annually. This is based on the assumption that natural gas would not provide a cheaper B.T.U. base. In view of the recent announcement in this house that a second natural gas line will commence construction shortly, a move which could eliminate the Hydro-Electric Power Board's need for coal to a bare minimum, the expected revenue from the transportation of coal could be eliminated.
I wonder whether the hon. member has heard of the study and research being conducted in respect of the movement of wheat and other commodities from western Canada
June 28, 1967	COMMONS
by pipe line. I regret that I do not have the figures showing the amount involved in this research but it is substantial. I venture to say that eventually pipe line transportation will be a major factor in covering the costs of moving merchandise over the long distances which we have in Canada.
Incidentally, according to figures the cost of transporting coal by rail compared with barge movement is as follows: For barge movement the cost per ton of coal is $3.65. In addition to the hauling of the barges there would be the cost of taking the coal from the mine to the water terminal, loading at the terminal, and carrying the five-month inventory at the power station for use in the winter months. While there are no definite figures on the cost of these operations they would probably total as much as the cost of the barge movement itself for an over-all total in the order of $6 to $7 per ton.
The present rail cost for a corresponding haul from pithead to power plant is estimated at $6 to $7 per ton. As hon. members can see there is little if any margin in favour of transporting coal by water rather than by rail in so far as Manitoba Hydro is concerned. Therefore the movement of coal by water might not occur at all, and even if it did coal would make no appreciable contribution in terms of transportation savings. The result would be that the savings which are necessary to justify the large capital outlay would need to be found in other traffic.
In so far as grain and petroleum products are concerned, there is nothing at present which indicates that the proposed water system would be competitive with present rail rates for grain and petroleum products moving eastward.
In summing up I might say that on the basis of these preliminary studies there would appear to be little justification for expenditures on works in the order of $100 million to $250 million in the interests of navigation on the Saskatchewan River. Hence it would seem doubtful that there is any reason to quarrel with the 1961 finding which was that a large outlay on engineering investigations is probably not warranted at this time. If it should be considered desirable some day to pursue the matter further, it is believed that studies should be made first of all on the economic side which would involve a more detailed analysis of traffic potential.
It may seem unpleasant to have to be realistic and dash cold water on such a romantic suggestion as a waterway through the heart of our great prairies. It would be much

Dr. Kuiper was of course referring not only to a waterway but to a full irrigation system that could be developed with it. Such a system, he said, would mean the end of drought for all time in the prairie provinces.
Dr. Kuiper's proposals were more ambitious than those of the hon. member for Selkirk (Mr. Stefanson). He also suggested the canalization of the Nelson River in northern Manitoba. Such a development, he said, would make it possible some day for Winnipeg residents to travel by boat deep into the heart of Alberta and for a change come back by a different route, through the Saskatchewan wheat fields to Hudson Bay. He said it would be a simple matter from a technical viewpoint to build ship locks in conjunction with future dams on the Saskatchewan and Nelson Rivers.
However, the results of the preliminary investigations I have described indicate, I believe, that although it may be simple from a technical viewpoint the capital expenditures involved would be very considerable, while the economic justification has not been firmly established in any of the investigations that have been carried out to date.

Mr. Speaker, I join the other speakers on this subject this afternoon who have said that it is one of great interest, particularly because in this centennial year the feat of the voyageurs who travelled over the route under discussion in opening up this country is being re-enacted. To anyone who was born on the prairies and lived in the west and absorbed some of its history, that was an era of wonderful adventure for Canadians and marked the greatest era of discovery in our history. It was an era of discovery which involved a water system longer, I believe, than the St. Lawrence, certainly stretching over a greater area.

It is probably not well known in eastern Canada that the Saskatchewan river system stretches literally over all the prairie lands to the foothills of the Rocky Mountains. It was on this great waterway that Alexander Mackenzie travelled in his voyages to discover a route to the Pacific. He arrived at Bella Coola and he painted on the side of a rock at that site the words "Alexander Mackenzie from Canada. By land. July 22, 1793."
It is interesting to consider his voyage from Montreal and the meaning of this waterway and its development in the terms which have been outlined by the hon. member for Fort William (Mr. Badanai) and the hon. member for Selkirk (Mr. Stefanson). We can follow this waterway again today with Mackenzie in order to gain some comprehension as to what its development could mean to the west and commercial traffic throughout that area. Alexander Mackenzie travelled from Montreal to the prairies. As I understand the history of his voyage it began above Lachine Rapids. His party moved in canoes up the Ottawa River. These canoes were approximately 30 to 35 feet in length. They were manned by six to eight men and carried freight loads weighing two, three or four tons. These canoes were known in the eastern section of this nation as "canot maitre," or master canoe, e (5:50 p.m.)
Alexander Mackenzie travelled the Ottawa River route rather than the St. Lawrence because of the difficulties with rapids he would have encountered. He negotiated the Chaudiere Falls and travelled above them on the Ottawa River to the Mattawa River. He then followed the Mattawa River to Lake Nipissing. He crossed Lake Nipissing and after portaging coasted down the French River to Georgian Bay. He went along the north shore of Georgian Bay following the canoe route to the north of Manitoulin Island and working his way westward he passed through the Straits of Mackinac and crossed lake Superior to the head of the lakes and what was known in those days as Grand Portage. This was the route that Radisson and Gro-seilliers had travelled in 1650. It was the route along which Marquette and Joliet had travelled on their original voyage of discovery to the headwaters of the Mississippi in 1673 and the same route over which LaSalle had gone when he made his voyage in 1682 across to the headwaters of the Mississippi and down that great river to its mouth.

Having reached Grand Rapids let us pause tor a moment to think of the feats of these voyageurs as they opened up the country. They made this trip involving approximately 36 portages from Montreal to the head of the lakes, some of them up to two miles in length, carrying canoes and loads on their backs of 200 pounds. One traveller who went with them tells of voyageurs who were loaded down with 200 pounds of freight on their backs, jigging along portages which caused these people to drop. These travellers wrote in their diaries that they could hardly keep up with the pace. They made these voyages in 35 to 40 days. There is an incident of a letter being taken from Montreal on May 6, 1817 and arriving at Grand Portage on June 3 in a canoe which was really an express canoe, not loaded with freight as the others were. This shows the speed at which mail and light freight could be portaged by these voyageurs as they moved westward.
From Grand Portage they moved through the maze of lakes, which was a very complicated process, through the wilderness leading to the prairies, and then took the route along Rainy River into Rainy Lake and thence into Lake of the Woods. Then they came to the mouth of the Winnipeg River leading into Lake Winnipeg. This was the historic route which La Verendrye and his sons had taken in 1731 when they moved across that country and out into the prairies for the first time. I might say they were not the first white people on the prairies because Henry Kelsey of the Hudson's Bay Company had gone there before coming down the northern route in 1690. At that time he went to the north end of Lake Winnipeg and into the mouth of the Saskatchewan River.
It is interesting to consider the long history of that river and its importance in the development of early Canada. In the early part of the eighteenth century these voyageurs were moving in considerable numbers west of Grand Portage or west of the head of the lakes, trans-shipping at this point into somewhat smaller canoes, the "canots du nord", or northern canoes. These were light canoes which could carry one or two tons of freight and were operated by a smaller crew. They

Establishment of Inland Waterway were manned by the elite of the voyageurs who at that time, in the middle of the eighteenth century, were moving far across the Canadian west. They followed a course up Lake Winnipeg, across Cedar Lake into the mouth of the Saskatchewan River and along the Saskatchewan River to the forks. They took the line of the North Saskatchewan from the forks and moved on to where the city of Edmonton now is and beyond. Then there were a series of portages and they made their way over into the Athabasca and coasted down the Athabasca to Slave lake where Fort Chippewa was established.
It was at Fort Chippewa that Alexander Mackenzie wintered during his historic voyage to the west. He tells in his diaries how imperative it was to the voyageur of that day in making the trip between the opening up of the rivers in the springtime and freeze-up in the fall to meet the rugged schedule from Montreal to the Great Lakes, thence across to the prairies and across the prairies to Fort Chippewa. There was little time to waste and little time to do anything else except bend to the paddle if they were to make it in time to winter at Fort Chippewa. To those who were left on the prairies during those harsh winters it was indeed a rough experience and often one which resulted in the death of these brave and intrepid men. Mackenzie broke camp in the spring and began his journey up the Peace River, taking the fork southward along the Parsnip River and made his way into the headwaters of the Fraser. Then he went down the Fraser river past where the cities of Prince George and Quesnel now stand and made his way across country to Bella Coola where he chalked his name on the rocks.
